summary: Children aged 8–9 learn dichotomous classification keys as a procedure: a sequence of yes/no questions about observable features that narrows a set of organisms down to a single identity, one binary split at a time. Two skills are developed — FOLLOWING a key (concrete) and BUILDING a valid key for 6–8 organisms (the harder relational step that requires anticipating how each question partitions the whole set). Teach following before building, use real local organisms, and make good questions concrete by contrasting a binary observable question ('Does it have a backbone?') with a vague one ('Is it big?'). Note that a good question must be binary and observable AND must actually divide the particular set being keyed.
misconceptions: Writing non-binary or vague questions ('What colour is it?', 'Is it nice?') that don't cleanly split the set.
Thinking a key identifies by matching a picture rather than by answering questions about features.
Believing there is only one 'correct' key for a set, rather than many valid keys built from different questions.
Building a key that leaves two organisms in the same endpoint (unresolved) and not noticing the ambiguity.

activities.title: Follow a branching key to name a mystery organism
steps: Receive a mystery minibeast (or leaf) and a branching yes/no key with 6–8 candidate organisms.
Read the first question (e.g. 'Does it have legs?'), check the actual feature on the specimen, and take the matching branch — do not skip ahead to guess a name.
Continue answering each question in order ('More than six legs?', 'Does it have wings?') and track which candidates remain after each split.
Stop when a single organism is left: that is the identification, provided the specimen is one of the organisms the key covers (check it against the endpoint's description).
Optionally use a live 'remaining candidates' strip that shrinks from all the key's creatures (6–8) to one as each answer is given, so the narrowing is visible.
activities.insight: A key identifies an organism by answering questions about its observable features one split at a time, not by matching it to a picture; each yes/no answer eliminates candidates until exactly one remains.

activities.title: Build your own yes/no key from a jumble of organisms
steps: Take 6–8 organisms and arrange them into a branching tree, authoring one yes/no question at each fork.
Choose questions that are binary and observable, that are unambiguous, and that actually divide the remaining set — ideally roughly in half.
Optionally use a two-column split table at each question (organisms answering yes | organisms answering no) so the partition is visible before committing to it.
Test the key by running every organism through it: a valid key sends each creature to its own unique endpoint.

Deliberately try a vague question such as 'Is it big?' and notice that different people may answer it differently for the same creature (big compared with what?), so the same organism can be sent down different branches and the key gives inconsistent results.

Rewrite the vague question as a binary observable feature that genuinely splits THIS set — e.g. 'Does it have wings?' or 'More than six legs?' for a minibeast set, or 'Does it have a backbone?' only when the set mixes vertebrates and invertebrates — then re-test. (A feature that sends every organism down the same branch, like 'Does it have a backbone?' for an all-invertebrate set, does not split the set.)
activities.insight: A key's questions must be binary, observable and unambiguous, and must divide the actual set so every organism reaches a unique endpoint; discovering that people disagree on a vague or subjective question, or that a non-splitting question leaves organisms unseparated, shows WHY such questions fail, not just that keys exist.

activities.title: Study and annotate a worked key, then stress-test it
steps: Examine a pre-built key for a familiar set (minibeasts or leaves), revealing at each branch the question and which organisms go left and right.
Describe aloud the STRUCTURE: every node is one yes/no question; every path leads to a single named organism.
Discuss whether there is only one 'correct' key, and try writing a different first question that still cleanly splits the same set.
Challenge the key: if a brand-new creature arrived that fits none of the endpoints, decide where a new question or branch would be added to fix it.
activities.insight: Many valid keys can be built from the same set using different questions; a key is a flexible tool, and it can be extended or repaired when a new organism does not fit any existing endpoint.

activities.title: 'Guess my organism' 20-questions warm-up
steps: Play a Socratic '20 questions' game: an adult (or peer) thinks of one organism and the child asks yes/no questions to identify it.
Keep a running list of candidate organisms and cross off those eliminated by each answer.
After the game, notice which questions eliminated the most candidates and discuss why binary, feature-based questions worked better than vague ones.
activities.insight: Narrowing a set by asking good yes/no questions is the same logic a key automates; question quality determines how quickly the set shrinks.

checkQuestion: Give the child pictures of 6–8 minibeasts (or leaves) and two jobs to DO while you watch. First: 'Use this branching key to name this unknown creature — show me each step as you go.' Then: 'Now make your own yes/no key so a friend could identify any one of these six creatures.' Watch how they choose questions and follow branches; do not explain the method or supply features.
checkAnswer: Following a key: reads each question, checks the actual feature on the specimen, and takes the correct branch in order until one organism remains — without skipping to a guessed name. Building a key: chooses observable, unambiguous yes/no features (e.g. 'Has wings?', 'More than six legs?') that divide the set, with each question narrowing the group so every organism ends at its own unique endpoint.
